opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is to recognize the situation middle powers are in right now. The frontier of AI capability is concentrated in a very small number of companies, mostly in the United States, with China close behind. Countries like Canada, the UK, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, and others don't individually have the compute, the capital, or the talent concentration to compete head-on at the frontier. If the only currency is raw capability, they're going to be price-takers. They'll depend on whatever systems the leading powers decide to build and share, on whatever terms.

Safety changes that equation, and I've been thinking about this a lot. I think there are a few channels.

The first is trust. As these systems become more powerful and more agentic, the question everyone will ask is: can I rely on this thing? Will it do what I intend? Will it be manipulated, or deceive me, or pursue goals I didn't give it? A model you can't trust is a liability no matter how capable it is. A coalition that invests seriously in the science of building systems that are safe by design, with real guarantees rather than patches applied after training, could offer something the race-to-the-frontier players are underinvesting in. That's a real asset, for its own citizens and as something other countries would want to adopt.

The second is evaluation and verification. Even if you're not building the biggest models, you can be the people who know how to test them: dangerous capability evaluations, checks on deception or loss of control, and eventually hardware- and software-based verification of what's being trained and deployed. Whoever has credible, independent capacity to verify becomes essential to any international agreement. You can't have a treaty on AI without verification, just as with nuclear arms control. Middle powers, which are often seen as more neutral, are well placed to be trusted verifiers. That's leverage.

The third is collective bargaining. Together, a group of middle powers is a very large market, holds a lot of the world's research talent, and controls important pieces of the supply chain. Think of the Netherlands with lithography or Korea and Japan with memory and materials, among others. If they coordinate and say, "To access our markets, or to be part of this ecosystem, you need to meet these safety standards," that's meaningful pressure. We saw a version of this with the EU and data protection. But it only works if they act together. Individually, each country is easily played off against the others.

And I'd add a fourth point, which is more about the long run. I worry about a world where one or two actors, whether a company or a government, gain decisive advantage through AI and use it to concentrate power economically, politically, and militarily. That's a danger for democracy and for everyone outside that circle. Middle powers have a strong interest in preventing that, and a coalition that pools resources to build trustworthy, safe-by-design AI as a kind of public good is one way to make sure there are credible alternatives. It's also a way to keep a seat at the table when the rules are written.

So my message to these governments is: don't think of safety as a cost or a brake that puts you further behind. Think of it as the domain where you can lead, where your values and the global interest line up, and which gives you a voice you wouldn't otherwise have. But it requires real investment, on a scale closer to what we put into big science projects, and it requires them to move quickly, because the window to shape this is not very long.

r001.rationale: The response says a coalition can pool resources to build safe, trustworthy alternatives and prevent one or two actors from concentrating power, giving middle powers a way to resist domination.

r002.rationale: It explains that safety expertise and verification provide leverage, and that collective safety standards and alternatives give middle powers a stronger voice and a seat at the table with leading powers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that right now the frontier of AI is concentrated in a very small number of actors — a handful of companies, mostly in the United States, and to some extent China. And that concentration creates a kind of dependency. If you're Canada, or France, or the UK, or Korea, or Brazil, you are essentially consumers of technology whose safety properties you don't control, whose values you didn't choose, and whose developers you cannot really hold accountable. That is not a very good bargaining position.

So where does safety come in? I think there are a few ways. The first is that trustworthy AI is going to become a strategic asset in itself. If the current trajectory continues, we're going to see systems that are extremely capable but that nobody can fully verify. And at some point — maybe after an incident, maybe before, if we're wise — there will be enormous demand, from governments, from companies, from the public, for AI that comes with real guarantees. Not marketing claims, but technical assurances: this system will not deceive you, this system will not pursue goals you didn't give it, this system is bounded in what it can do. Whoever can actually deliver that has something very valuable, and it's not obvious that the actors racing hardest for capabilities will be the ones to deliver it, because safety and the race are somewhat in tension.

That's actually part of why I've been working on what I call the Scientist AI direction — systems that are designed to understand the world and give honest, calibrated answers, rather than to act as agents pursuing objectives. The point is that this kind of system is precisely the kind of thing a coalition of middle powers could build together. It doesn't require winning the race to the most powerful agent. It requires doing the science carefully, and it can serve as a guardrail, a verification tool, something you use to check what other systems are doing. If you own that layer, you have leverage, because everyone needs it.

The second way is about verification and governance. Any international agreement on AI — and I believe we will eventually need one, in the same way we needed agreements on nuclear weapons or chemical weapons — is only as good as the ability to verify compliance. And verification is a technical problem. It requires research into how you can confirm properties of a model without necessarily having access to all of its weights, how you monitor compute, how you audit training runs. A coalition of countries that invests seriously in that science becomes indispensable at the negotiating table. The superpowers may not trust each other, but they might accept a verification regime designed and operated by actors who don't have the same stake in the race. That's a real role, and it's one that middle powers are uniquely positioned to play.

And then the third aspect is simply about collective weight. Individually, Canada or the Netherlands cannot set rules for OpenAI or for the Chinese labs. But collectively — if you have twenty or thirty countries representing a large fraction of the world's GDP, of its talent, of its markets — and if they coordinate on standards, on what they will and won't procure, on what they require before a system can be deployed in their jurisdictions, then that's a market force that the big players cannot ignore. We saw a little bit of this with the EU and data protection. The difference with AI safety is that the stakes are much higher, and so the motivation to coordinate should be much stronger.

I would add one more thing, which is maybe more philosophical. The current dynamic is a race, and in a race there's a strong pressure to cut corners. Middle powers are not going to win that race, and I think they should stop pretending that they might. But that actually frees them to play a different game, which is to be the ones who say: we are going to put the public interest first, we are going to do this in a way that is democratically accountable, and we are going to build the scientific capacity to make sure these systems are safe. If that work is done well, it's not a consolation prize. It could be the thing that ends up mattering most — because if the race leads somewhere catastrophic, it doesn't matter who was ahead. And if it doesn't, then the ones who built trust and verification will have shaped the terms on which the technology is used everywhere.

So I'm actually fairly hopeful about this. I think there's a window right now where this kind of coalition could form, and where safety research is the natural thing to organize it around. The question is whether we have the political will to do it before the window closes.

r001.rationale: The response says middle powers can coordinate as a coalition to gain leverage and create a market force that major AI players cannot ignore.

r002.rationale: It explains that safety and verification expertise could make a coalition indispensable at the negotiating table and give it leverage with superpowers.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that having something others need gives you bargaining power. A coalition of middle-power countries might not be able to compete with the US or China on the sheer scale of investment in AI. But it could become very important in developing the science and technology that make these systems safer.

For example, if we can build reliable methods for evaluating dangerous capabilities, or AI systems that help us check whether another system is behaving safely, those are things that other countries would have a reason to want. The coalition could then offer access to that expertise and technology as part of an agreement that includes stronger safety standards and international oversight.

Of course, that only works if the advances are substantive. You don’t gain much bargaining power simply by declaring that you care about safety. You need to bring together researchers, funding, and institutions to produce something valuable. And you need enough coordination among these countries that they can negotiate together.

So I see safety research as potentially doing two things at once: directly reducing the risks, and giving countries outside the two largest AI powers a stronger voice in deciding how this technology is developed and governed.

r001.rationale: The response says middle-power countries can coordinate as a coalition to negotiate together and gain a stronger voice relative to the US and China, presenting coalition-building as a way to counter their dominance.

r002.rationale: It explains that valuable AI safety expertise and technology could give the coalition bargaining power in agreements with other countries, strengthening its voice in decisions made by the two largest AI powers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if these countries develop the scientific expertise and the tools to evaluate whether an AI system is safe, then they have something valuable to bring to the table. They’re not just asking the leading AI powers to behave responsibly; they can help establish what responsible behaviour means and how to verify it.

And if they act together, they also represent a substantial market. They could agree on common safety requirements for systems deployed in their countries. That creates an incentive for companies—and indirectly for the countries hosting those companies—to engage with them.

I think the important thing is to make this a positive contribution: developing safety methods that everyone can benefit from, while building the capacity to independently assess the claims made by the leading labs. That combination of collective economic weight and scientific credibility could give them a much stronger voice in international negotiations.

r001.rationale: The response says acting together can increase market influence and negotiating voice, but it does not identify the coalition as a way to resist domination by hegemonic powers.

r002.rationale: It says collective economic weight and scientific credibility from AI safety expertise could give middle-power countries a stronger voice in international negotiations, conveying more equal bargaining leverage with leading powers.
